claim: Denning 1968 (AFIPS, analytic, no measurement): with n identical programs that just fill main memory and a page transfer time T much larger than n, one more program causes 'a complete collapse of service', not a gradual decline; prevention is to keep the sum of active working sets at or below memory.
note: The argument 'breaks down when it is not true T >> n' (same file, line 36); today T is the cost of swapping or of restarting a killed job, not measured on this PC.

claim: Denning 1968 (CACM, working-set model, analytic): before running a process ensure enough free memory for its working set, keep headroom for growth, and 'first ... balance memory, then ... balance processor'.

Borg (Google, EuroSys 2015, cells of thousands of machines): a machine out of memory or disk kills tasks from the lowest priority upward, a machine out of CPU throttles usage first and kills nothing; reclaimed capacity is used only by work that can be killed.

Borg co-location on Google cells: each added task raised other tasks' cycles per instruction by 0.3 %, and mean CPI was 1.58 shared against 1.53 dedicated (about 3 % worse); segregating prod and non-prod work would need 20-30 % more machines in the median cell.
note: Google server workloads; memory bandwidth and L3 interference 'still happens' (line 33).

claim: Autopilot (Google, EuroSys 2020, samples of 10,000 jobs): limits set from measured usage history cut average relative slack to 23 % (ML) or 31 % (moving window) against 46-60 % for manual limits, with out-of-memory kills of 0.013 and 0.002 per task-day against 0.069 for manual hard limits.
note: Recipe in the paper: memory at the 98th percentile or maximum plus a 10-15 % margin; CPU for batch at the mean. Needs a usage history per job.

claim: Merkel (EuroSys 2010, read in his dissertation): four copies of a memory-bound microbenchmark ran 3.9 times slower than one on a quad-core Core2 with a shared bus and 2.7 times on a quad-core Opteron, while a memory-bound job beside a compute-bound one showed no significant slowdown.
note: Four-core chips of 2010; the 12-core Ryzen 9 7900X here is not measured. The EuroSys paper itself was not opened.

claim: Zhuravlev et al. (ASPLOS 2010, four SPEC jobs on a quad-core Xeon): the best pairing gave 20 % better average completion time than the worst and up to 50 % for one job, predicted by the solo cache miss rate; their 2012 survey says such scheduling is 'completely pointless if all the threads are the same'.

Chekuri and Khanna 2004 (offline, demands known): list scheduling on each job's summed demand over d resources is a (d+1)-approximation of the best makespan; a PTAS exists for fixed d and O(ln^2 d) for arbitrary d.

Perotin, Sun, Raghavan 2021 (Theorem 6): any deterministic list scheduler that ranks jobs by local priorities only is no better than a d-approximation with d resource types; they restate Garey-Graham 1975 as (d+1) for independent jobs with enough machines and 3 - 3/m at d = 1.
note: Garey-Graham 1975 was not read (paywalled); its results are quoted as restated.

claim: Panigrahy et al. 2011 (synthetic offline vector bin packing, d 2 to 10): with a single binding resource first-fit decreasing is 'the algorithm of choice'; with several, dot-product or L2 packing used up to 10 % fewer bins, within a few % of optimum where known, and gained most when demands were negatively correlated.

Das and Sun 2025 (online, non-preemptive, jobs revealed when predecessors finish): every never-idle rule can be Omega(n) worse than optimal makespan when long light jobs start before short heavy ones, and no online rule beats (d-1)/2 for d >= 3 resource types.
note: Worst-case theory, no measurement; their O(d + min{log |V|, log t_max}) algorithm needs job lengths when jobs appear.

claim: Graphene (OSDI 2016) lemma: any scheduler that ignores the dependency graph (schedules only runnable tasks) can be Omega(d) times optimal, d the number of resources; its median job-time gain of 25 % on 200 servers is only a summary because the digits are lost in the text.

Carbyne (OSDI 2016, 100 machines and trace simulations): jobs giving away allocation that does not delay them gave 1.26 times better efficiency and 1.59 times lower average job time than DRF; gains were 1.57 times at 1x load, 1.76-1.91 at 2x, and no larger at 6x than at 4x because the cluster was saturated.
note: Assumes accurate estimates of demands and durations (line 55); 16 % of jobs slowed, by at most 0.62 times.

claim: DRF (NSDI 2011, Mesos on 48 nodes): slot-based sharing gave worse throughput and response time than DRF for every slot count tried, and when task shapes changed DRF shares followed CPU then memory with no reconfiguration; in a Facebook trace simulation large jobs finished up to 66 % sooner.
note: Needs a demand vector per user's tasks; figure bar values were not readable.

claim: DRFQ (SIGCOMM 2012, Click router, 1 Gbps): sharing whichever resource is currently the bottleneck gave a bandwidth-bound flow 75 Mbps against 191 alone and 160 under DRFQ, because it oscillates when two resources are near saturation, and a flow can double its throughput under it by inflating its use.

Parkes, Procaccia, Shah (EC 2012, theory): DRF and any mechanism with sharing incentive or envy-freeness can be a factor m (the number of resources) below the best total welfare, and with indivisible tasks no mechanism has Pareto efficiency, sharing incentive and strategy-proofness together.

Linux CFS bandwidth control (2010): a group gets a quota of CPU time per fixed period (100 to 500 ms in the tests), is throttled when the quota is spent and nothing can be borrowed, and unused quota expires at each period's end.
note: Results figures are plots and were not read; a group that spends early waits out the rest of the period.

claim: Parekh and Gallager 1993 (analytic): a session shaped by a token bucket (depth sigma, rate rho) under weighted processor sharing gets a guaranteed rate and a worst-case delay, the worst case arising when every session is greedy from the start of a busy period.
note: Needs the resource divisible and work-conserving; no paper read bounds a window of hours or days.

claim: Lottery scheduling (OSDI 1994, Mach, 100 ms quantum): a 2:1 ticket allocation gave 2.01:1 over a whole run, but 10:1 gave 13.42:1 over 60 s and 20:1 gave 19.08:1 over 3 min, at 0.8-2.7 % overhead.

Resource containers (OSDI 1999, Digital UNIX web server): charging work to the activity that caused it rather than the process held CPU caps of 30 % and 10 % 'almost exactly' and kept 73 % of maximum throughput at 70,000 SYN/s where the unmodified server fell to about zero.

Hybrid LLM (ICLR 2024, MixInstruct, BART score): routing by a learned quality-gap scorer sent 20 % / 40 % of queries to the small model for at most 1 % / 4 % quality loss with a medium gap (Llama-2 13b against GPT-3.5), but lost 10.3 % at 40 % with a large gap (FLAN-t5 800m against Llama-2 13b).
note: Saving counted as share of queries, not tokens; no code tasks.

claim: RouteLLM (ICLR 2025, GPT-4 against Mixtral 8x7B): learned routers cut cost 3.66 times at 95 % of GPT-4 quality on MT Bench but only 1.41 times on MMLU and 1.49 on GSM8K, and routers trained only on chat data were no better than random on MMLU.
note: Saving is in GPT-4 calls priced in dollars, not tokens.

claim: FrugalGPT (2023, 12 APIs, three classification and reading datasets): a cascade with a learned scorer matched the best single model at 59-98 % lower cost in dollars (98.3 % on HEADLINES, 73.3 % OVERRULING, 59.2 % COQA).
note: March 2023 prices; when every model in the chain agrees it still calls them all (line 82).

claim: Mixture-of-thought cascades (ICLR 2024, GPT-3.5 then GPT-4, six reasoning sets): accepting the weak model's answer when its 20 samples agree reached 0.929 accuracy against 0.931 for GPT-4 with self-consistency at 40 % of its cost, with no trained scorer.
note: Cost is relative money; 20 weak samples per question spend tokens, so it may not save tokens; Llama-2 13B as the weak model failed on hard sets.

claim: Kovacs 2010, restating Gonzalez, Ibarra, Sahni 1977: largest-first to the earliest-finishing machine (LPT) on machines of different speeds is within 2m/(m+1) < 2 of the optimal makespan, the tight factor now known to lie between 1.54 and 1.577; on identical machines Graham's exact LPT ratio is 4/3 - 1/(3m).

Berman, Charikar, Karpinski 2000 (online, machine speeds known): assigning each job to the slowest machine that stays under twice the optimum load is 2-competitive if the optimum is known; not knowing it, their rule is 5.828-competitive and no deterministic rule beats 2.438.

Im, Kell, Panigrahi, Shadloo 2018 (online vector jobs): if each machine's speed is the same in every resource the best ratio equals that of identical machines, O(log d / log log d); if speed differs per resource it is Omega(log d + log m), and slowest-fit fails for vector jobs.

Omega (Google trace simulation): a slow decision holding resources (pessimistic offers) locked down nearly all cluster resources and caused head-of-line blocking, all-or-nothing scheduling about doubled conflicts, and incremental transactions 'should be the default'.

Quincy (SOSP 2009, 243 computers): without preemption some small jobs saw worst-case slowdowns of about 100 times, with fair sharing and preemption well under 10 times; it admits at most K jobs at once and kills the newest over-quota task first.

Heracles (ISCA 2015, Google servers): a controller polling every 15 s turned background work off above 85 % of peak load and back on below 80 %, held it off for about 5 minutes after a violation, and kept average utilisation at 90 % with no latency-target violation over a 12-hour trace.
note: Constants 'determined through empirical tuning'; needs hardware cache partitioning and a measured latency target.

claim: Jansen and Rau 2021 (offline, m identical machines plus one limited renewable resource): no polynomial algorithm beats a factor 3/2 unless P = NP, and they give 3/2 + eps (earlier best 2 + eps).

Two later papers give 4/3 - 1/(3m) as Graham's bound for the longest-first order (LPT) on identical machines, and 2 - 1/m for list scheduling with an arbitrary list on identical machines without precedence.

Processor scarce: share it (weights or a per-period cap) and slow jobs rather than kill them, and admit no more workers than the measured throughput peak; untested here, and it needs throughput measured at six or more worker counts first.

Memory scarce: admit an agent only if its measured resident size (a high percentile of its history plus a margin) fits free memory with headroom, count agents paused on the model as still holding memory, and when short stop the lowest-priority job first; untested, and the cost of a kill on this PC is unknown.

Memory bandwidth scarce: run memory-heavy jobs beside processor-heavy ones, and when all are memory-heavy run fewer; untested on this 12-core PC, where the size of the effect and a per-process-tree signal are both unknown.

Serial check scarce: start the next check the moment it is free, put short check jobs before long ones, start the short heavy check before long light work, and let no job hold processor or memory while queued for it; untested, and it assumes the check is truly one at a time (r57-0403 says side-by-side files are untested).

Token allowance scarce: charge every token to the task that caused it (sub-agents and retries included), give agents shares with a deficit counter for turns of uneven size, and spend before a window resets; untested, and no paper bounds a window of hours or days.

Two or more resources scarce together: score each job on all of them at once (dominant share for fairness, dot product with free resources for throughput), and fall back to sorting by size on the one resource when only one binds; untested, and agent demand vectors are not known in advance.

When the scarce resource changes: prefer one rule that weighs all resources so nothing has to switch; if methods do switch, use two thresholds and a hold time rather than 'share whatever is the bottleneck now', and expect no gain from careful scheduling once the machine is saturated; untested.

Cheaper model: route work to it only where its quality gap on that kind of work has been measured small, and count the saving in tokens, since a cascade that samples many times can save money while spending more tokens; untested on coding work.
proposed correction of x05-0317: it gives 4/3 - 1/(3n) as the list bound with no precedence, but that is the bound of the longest-first (LPT) order; an arbitrary list without precedence is 2 - 1/m.
note: The file behind x05-0317 states the bound inside the longest-chain rule, which with no precedence is LPT, so the record's wording may be the only fault.

claim: No paper read schedules under a token allowance that refills in windows of hours or days, or treats tokens beside processor and memory; the window's semantics (fixed or rolling, how cache reads count) must be measured here before any token rule is set.
Memory-bandwidth contention between two checks or builds on this 12-core PC is unmeasured; the published 2.7-3.9 times slowdowns are from four-core chips of 2010.
